entities.summary:
The Ajanta Caves are 30 rock-cut Buddhist cave monuments in Maharashtra, India, dating from the 2nd century BCE to the 6th century CE. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, they contain extraordinary paintings and sculptures considered the finest surviving examples of ancient Indian art, depicting the life of the Buddha, Jataka tales, and scenes from Gupta-era India.

The caves were created in two distinct periods: the Hinayana phase (2nd-1st century BCE) created basic chaitya prayer halls and viharas (monk residences); the Mahayana phase (5th-6th century CE) under Gupta patronage produced the magnificent painted caves with vibrant murals using mineral pigments, lime plaster, and extraordinary artistic skill. The paintings' preservation for 1,500+ years in sealed, dark caves created a time capsule of ancient Indian aesthetics.

Abandoned around 650 CE and forgotten by the local population, the caves were rediscovered in 1819 by a British officer, John Smith, while tiger hunting. His graffiti ('John Smith, 28th Cavalry') is still visible near cave 10. The rediscovery triggered global scholarly interest and conservation efforts. The Ajanta murals influenced medieval Indian art, Sri Lankan Buddhist painting at Sigiriya, and provided evidence of Gupta-era Indian culture's sophistication, refuting colonial narratives of Indian stagnation.
